items.title: Joe Wilder Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: The first big band I played with, a name orchestra, was Les Hite. I played in that band

ctx.x: How about your first big band experience? You’ve played in so many big bands.

The first big band I played with, a name orchestra, was Les Hite. I played in that band and during the time I was in that band Dizzy Gillespie also joined it, Britt Woodman was the first trombone player, and Gerald Wiggins, Britt Woodman and his brother Coney, who was our pianist, were drafted at the same time. And Gerald Wiggins joined the band. He was in the band at the time Dizzy Gillespie was in the band for a short time.
Did you get to do some traveling at that point, around the country, did you travel?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: I ended up for instance in Les Hite’s band... I was actually in awe of most of the fellows who were in those bands... When I left Les Hite I joined the Lionel Hampton band

ctx.x: I wanted to ask you about when you were with the couple of big bands before the Marines, and then after again, can you recall if you had a goal? An eventual goal for your music career at that point?

You know I was so thrilled in a way and surprised too that I ended up for instance in Les Hite’s band because I was 19 years old and this was quite an experience for me, and I remember when I left Philadelphia on a bus to go to Lansing, Michigan to join Les Hite’s band and my mother accompanied me to the bus terminal, and I can remember my mother standing, as I had the window down and the bus is loaded with people, and my mother saying, “don’t you do anything to embarrass this family while you’re away.” And I…

rather surprised and I was actually in awe of most of the fellows who were in those bands. They were a little older than me. Some of them were in my age group but a lot of them were older and had a lot more experience. So I felt kind of lucky to be there. When I left Les Hite I joined the Lionel Hampton band, which at that time was roaring, and I was really in awe of that band. I mean I was again quite happy that I became a member. But it’s strange because the first trumpet player was Carl George and he was…

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got a call to go with Les Hite. That’s why I joined the Les Hite band out in Lansing, Michigan.

ctx.x: So in high school, then, you were playing in the band and you were – what happened when you graduated? What did you decide to do?

I started playing with – I got a call to go out. I played with several bands in Philadelphia at the same time I was in school. I played with Jimmy Gorham’s band. The first band, oddly enough – I played with a man called King Coleman. He was a friend of my father’s. He was a pianist. He had a little society group. It wasn’t a band. It was a group. He gave me the first chance to start trying to play and trying to learn to improvise, which was – I didn’t really understand, but I could read some of the melodic lines.…

and they wanted me to join that band. I quit the other band and joined them. My father said, “Yeah, but you’re not going to make any money over there, playing with Jimmy Gorham. You’re working with Mr. Sadler, and he pays you well” and so on and so on. “No, that’s not the thing to do. That’s not hep enough for me.” I had to go with this other band. So I played with them for a while. Then I finished with them, and I played with a band called the Harlem Dictators. There was a fine trumpet player in there, Frank…

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Yeah. I was 19 in Les’s band.

ctx.x: Then you joined Les Hite’s band. You were 19 years old.
Yeah. I was 19 in Les’s band.
A young kid. What was that like? I’ve heard that you were a little embarrassed when you got on the bus, because your mom was there.
